lines.text: A long lake in the Great Rift Valley, an old kingdom, a British protectorate and a young democracy. This is the story of Malawi.
Thousands of years ago, hunters and later farmers painted the rock shelters of Chongoni, now a World Heritage Site.
From the late 1400s, the Maravi kingdom ruled the shores of the lake. The country would one day take its name from it.
In 1859, the Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached the lake and campaigned against the slave trade he found there.
Hastings Banda, a doctor born in 1890, would lead Malawi to independence, and then rule it for thirty years.
In 1902, a small settlement was founded at Lilongwe. It would become the capital in 1975.
In 1907, the land became the British protectorate of Nyasaland.
In 1915, the preacher John Chilembwe led a rising against colonial rule. It was crushed, but he is remembered as a hero.
Peter Mutharika, born in 1940, would serve as president twice, from 2014 and again from 2025.
Joyce Banda, born in 1950, would become the first woman to lead Malawi.
In 1964, Nyasaland became independent as Malawi. After Banda's long rule, Malawians voted for multi-party democracy in 1994.
In 1980, part of the lake became a national park, home to hundreds of kinds of brightly coloured cichlid fish.
From painted rocks to a free vote, Malawi's story runs on along its great lake.
